Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by having a small draft model propose k tokens at a time, which the target model then verifies or rejects in a single forward pass — the speedup lives entirely in the rejection rate staying low. The central question here is: when prompts shift to a domain the draft model handles worse than the target model (e.g., a small general-purpose draft paired with a code-specialized target on legal text), how quickly does the acceptance rate degrade, and is that degradation smooth or cliff-like? The key concepts are the token-level acceptance probability α (typically estimated per-position under the speculative sampling correction), the KL divergence between draft and target distributions as a proxy for mismatch, and how domain shift interacts with vocabulary skew — rare domain tokens the draft assigns near-zero probability to cause cascading rejections because a single rejection voids the entire suffix of the proposal. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is that aggregate metrics like mean acceptance rate are deeply misleading: a draft that accepts 90% of tokens on average can still deliver near-zero wall-clock speedup if rejections cluster at early positions in the proposal window, forcing frequent short accepts and wasting the batched verification cost. The subtler danger is that capacity mismatch under domain shift doesn't just lower α uniformly — it distorts the position-conditional acceptance curve in ways that interact badly with the chosen speculation length k, making the optimal k itself a moving target that naive deployments never re-tune.

The root cause is prefix probability collapse: when the draft model assigns low probability to the first out-of-distribution token in a domain-shifted context, it poisons every downstream position because speculative sampling under the Leviathan et al. This happens specifically when the draft's conditional distribution at position 1 is miscalibrated in entropy: the draft is overconfident (low entropy, wrong mode) on the first domain-shifted token rather than uncertain, because overconfidence maximally inflates the rejection probability term. A concrete example: pair a 125M GPT-2-family draft with LLaMA-3-70B on biomedical text — the draft will confidently predict common English continuations after a Latin medical term, producing p_draft near 1.0 for the wrong token while p_target is near 0.0, yielding near-certain rejection at position 1 on nearly every proposal. To detect this before deployment, you should measure the position-conditional acceptance curve — compute α(position=j) separately for j=1…k on a held-out domain sample — and look for a convex shape (steep drop at j=1, flat afterward) rather than the concave or uniform shape you'd see with healthy draft-target alignment. A sharper pre-deployment signal is the draft entropy vs. target entropy correlation at position 1 across domain prompts: if the draft is systematically lower-entropy than the target on your target domain (Spearman ρ < 0.3 is a reasonable alarm threshold empirically), you have overconfident-wrong-mode pathology and should either reduce k aggressively or switch drafts. Chen et al.'s SpecBench (2024) implicitly surfaces this when draft efficiency collapses on coding vs. chat splits even with the same draft-target pair — the mechanism is exactly this position-1 miscalibration rather than uniform accuracy degradation.

If you wanted to make the draft model robust to domain shift without retraining it, what inference-time interventions could you apply to its distribution — and what are the precise failure modes of each?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1878)

The most direct intervention is temperature scaling the draft upward — raising draft temperature from 1.0 to 1.3–1.6 flattens its distribution, reducing overconfident wrong-mode predictions and lowering the 1 − p_target/p_draft rejection term at position 1; the failure mode is that higher temperature also flattens correct high-confidence predictions, so on in-distribution prefixes you're actively degrading acceptance rate by spreading probability mass away from tokens the target also favors, and there's no per-token signal telling you when to apply it. A more targeted intervention is draft logit truncation via top-p or top-k restriction loosening — widening the draft's sampling nucleus forces probability mass onto lower-ranked tokens the target might prefer, but the failure mode is that on long proposals this increases the variance of accepted token quality, and because the speculative correction is designed for the untruncated draft distribution, you're now running the acceptance test against a distribution that doesn't match what you actually sampled from, creating a subtle validity violation that biases the joint distribution away from the target. Contrastive decoding-inspired draft adjustment — subtracting a smaller "amateur" model's logits from the draft at inference time (Li et al., 2022 style) — can suppress the generic completions the draft overweights on domain-shifted text, but requires a third model and fails when the domain shift affects tokens that neither the draft nor the amateur model has strong opinions about, leaving the miscalibration untouched. Retrieval-augmented draft priming — prepending retrieved in-domain passages to the draft's context window without changing the target's context — cheaply shifts the draft's prior toward domain vocabulary, and this actually works reasonably well for lexical domain shift (legal, biomedical); the failure mode is semantic domain shift where the relevant adaptation isn't vocabulary but reasoning structure (e.g., chain-of-thought math), where retrieved text doesn't reshape the draft's position-1 distribution in the ways that matter. The deepest failure mode shared by all inference-time interventions is that they operate on the draft's output distribution without access to the target's distribution at draft time, so they're essentially open-loop corrections — you cannot know at draft proposal time whether a given intervention helped or hurt on a specific token without running the target forward pass, which defeats the latency purpose of speculative decoding entirely.

You can construct such a scheme by treating each accept/reject outcome as a Bernoulli bandit signal and maintaining a lightweight logit bias vector over the draft's vocabulary that is updated online via a multiplicative weights / exponentiated gradient rule — when token x is rejected at position j, you downweight its logit by η·log(p_target(x)/p_draft(x)), where p_target(x) is revealed for free at verification time under the standard speculative sampling correction. This is theoretically grounded: the reject step already computes the likelihood ratio p_target/p_draft for the proposed token, so you get an unbiased gradient of the KL divergence at that position without any additional target forward passes, and the update is O(vocab_size) in the worst case but O(1) if you maintain sparse per-token counters. The convergence limit is brutal, however: rejections at position 1 are your primary signal, but under a healthy speculation length of k=4–8, you get at most one rejection signal per proposal window, and if α≈0.7 (typical for well-matched pairs), you're only observing ~30% of windows as informative update events — on a 500-token generation you accumulate perhaps 20–40 usable gradient steps, which is far too few to adapt a bias vector over a 32K–128K vocabulary without aggressive regularization or strong priors. The position-bias problem compounds this: since position-1 rejections dominate, your bias vector learns to correct early-position errors but remains blind to miscalibrations at positions 2…k that would matter if position-1 improved, creating a sequential debiasing bottleneck where fixing one position unmasks the next, requiring O(k) phases of adaptation each needing its own sample budget. The closest realized system is online speculative decoding explored in the context of REST (He et al., 2023) and lookahead decoding, where retrieved n-gram drafts are implicitly re-ranked by acceptance history — but these sidestep the sparse-signal problem by operating over n-gram keys rather than full vocabulary distributions, trading expressivity for sample efficiency. The theoretical floor on convergence rate is set by the accept/reject process being a Markov reward process with partial observability: you never see what the accepted counterfactual would have been for rejected tokens at positions j>1, so the effective sample complexity scales as O(k·vocab_size / (α_min · ε²)) for ε-accurate bias correction, which for realistic parameters runs into the millions of tokens — longer than most practical inference sessions.

You can force exploration of deeper positions by replacing the standard sequential draft with a stochastic skip proposal: with probability ε at each position j, sample the draft token from the target's distribution (obtained via a cheap approximate proxy, or simply from a uniform fallback) rather than the draft model, guaranteeing that position j+1 is reached and its miscalibration becomes observable regardless of what the draft would have done at j. The distribution-preservation question is the critical one, and the answer is yes with modification: the standard Leviathan et al. correction assumes the draft proposes from a fixed known distribution q(x), so if you replace q at position j with a mixture (1−ε)·q_draft + ε·q_explore, you must run the acceptance test against this mixture distribution rather than q_draft alone — the math goes through cleanly because the correction only requires that the proposal distribution be known and fixed per token, not that it come from any particular model. The failure mode is that ε-forced tokens at position j are accepted with probability min(1, p_target(x)/q_mixture(x)), and if q_explore is uniform over 128K vocabulary, q_mixture(x) for a correct token is inflated by ε/128000, which is negligible — but if q_explore is a poorly chosen proxy that assigns high mass to wrong tokens, you actively inject bad proposals that the acceptance test must then reject, wasting verification budget. A smarter explore distribution is target-proxy sampling: use the draft's top-k tokens but resample among them proportional to inverse draft-confidence, concentrating exploration on positions where the draft is uncertain-but-wrong rather than uniformly random, reducing wasted rejections while still exposing position j+1. The provable guarantee survives as long as the full mixture q_mixture has support wherever p_target has support — the standard absolute continuity condition — which uniform or top-k exploration satisfies trivially but domain-restricted exploration (e.g., only biomedical vocabulary) can violate, breaking the correctness proof in exactly the edge cases where domain shift is most severe. Empirically, ε in the range 0.05–0.15 is likely the practical operating point: small enough that forced-explore tokens don't dominate proposal cost, large enough that in a k=6 window you expect 0.3–0.9 forced explorations per proposal, giving you signal from deeper positions within tens rather than hundreds of generation steps.

response:
Non-stationarity does break the exact guarantee: the Leviathan et al. correctness proof requires that q(x_j) used in the acceptance ratio p_target(x_j)/q(x_j) is the same distribution that actually generated x_j, and if the bias vector has been updated between proposal and verification — even by a single gradient step — the denominator is wrong, producing a biased acceptance test that neither correctly samples from p_target nor from any other well-defined distribution. The damage is quantifiable: if the bias vector shifts by Δ in L∞ norm between proposal and verification, the total variation distance between the actual output distribution and p_target is bounded by O(k·exp(Δ)·ε) where ε is the base mismatch — small Δ means the corruption is proportional to speculation length k, so longer proposals amplify the distributional error multiplicatively, which is the worst possible interaction with the very mechanism meant to provide speedup. The weakest guarantee you can still provide is a per-window approximate correctness bound: if you freeze the bias vector during each proposal-verify cycle and only update it between windows, the distribution within each window is exactly correct conditioned on the bias state at proposal time, and the output sequence samples from a mixture of p_target-variants indexed by the evolving bias — this is not p_target, but it is a mixture of distributions each of which has the same support as p_target, which rules out the most pathological failures like never sampling certain tokens. A slightly stronger guarantee comes from framing the online adaptation as quasi-static: if the bias vector's L1 update magnitude per window is bounded by δ, you can show the KL divergence between actual output and p_target accumulates as O(T·δ²) over T windows, analogous to the regret bounds in online convex optimization (Hazan, 2016) — slow adaptation keeps the distributional drift controlled even though exact correctness is lost. The practical engineering resolution is snapshot verification: record q_draft(x_j) at proposal time using the current bias vector, store it alongside the proposal, and run the acceptance test against the stored q rather than recomputing from the now-updated bias — this restores exact correctness at the cost of O(k) extra memory per window to cache the proposal probabilities, which is negligible (k·4 bytes per float for k≤8). This snapshot approach is implicitly what any correct implementation must do, and the fact that most speculative decoding codebases don't explicitly address it reveals a latent bug in any system that attempts online draft adaptation without careful probability caching.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1882)
response:
Per-request bias vectors are cheap in isolation — a vocabulary-sized float32 vector over 128K tokens is 512KB, so 64 concurrent requests costs 32MB, negligible against the draft model's own parameter footprint — but the interaction with the batched forward pass is where the cost explodes: the draft model produces a single logit tensor of shape (batch_size, vocab_size), and applying per-request bias vectors requires an elementwise add of a (batch_size, vocab_size) bias matrix, which is a memory-bandwidth-bound operation that at batch_size=64 and vocab=128K moves 32MB of bias data per forward pass, added to every layer's activation traffic and potentially doubling memory pressure on the draft model's decode step. The more fundamental problem is that per-request bias vectors break the batched acceptance test: in standard batched speculative decoding (as implemented in systems like vLLM's draft-model speculator and TensorRT-LLM's speculative path), the verification step compares p_target and q_draft tensors that are naturally aligned across the batch — but with per-request q_draft(x_j) now depending on a request-specific bias state, you must either store per-request proposal probabilities at snapshot time (restoring correctness but requiring (batch_size × k) cached scalars, trivially cheap) or recompute per-request q_draft during verification, which requires re-running the bias application per request and defeats batching efficiency. The comparison to separate draft instances is instructive: a separate 125M-parameter draft per request at batch_size=64 would require 64×500MB = 32GB just for weights, which is clearly untenable, whereas per-request bias vectors add only 32MB total — so on pure memory, bias vectors win by three orders of magnitude. However, the compute cost comparison is subtler: a batched draft forward pass over 64 requests costs roughly the same FLOPs as a single request (batching is nearly free for memory-bound small models up to the point where compute becomes the bottleneck), while per-request bias application adds O(batch_size × vocab_size) work that scales linearly with batch size and cannot be amortized, meaning at large batch sizes the bias application can actually exceed the draft model's own forward pass cost. The practical resolution used in systems like Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024) — which maintain per-request draft heads rather than per-request bias vectors — suggests the field has converged on parameter-sharing with request-specific lightweight adapters as the right abstraction, where the shared draft backbone runs in one batched pass and per-request adaptation is applied via low-rank (rank-4 to rank-16) residual terms that cost O(batch_size × rank × vocab_size) rather than O(batch_size × vocab_size), recovering most of the batching efficiency while preserving per-request specialization.

The practical implication is that optimal draft selection is not monotone in draft domain expertise: you don't simply want the draft that performs best on your target domain in isolation, you want the draft whose distribution is most subordinate to the target's — meaning its probability mass is a subset of the target's high-probability region — which is a fundamentally different criterion than standalone accuracy and explains why generalist drafts often outperform specialist ones when paired with large generalist targets even on specialized domains.
